title: NaN != NaN, and Python's max() picks a different "largest" value depending on where the NaN sits in the list
assumption: max() and min() over a list of numbers return the mathematically largest/smallest value, regardless of order, and a value always equals itself.

input.description: A price list, exchange-rate feed, or sensor reading where a bad or missing value has been coerced to NaN (e.g. a failed `float()` parse or a 0/0 division) and then run through max()/min() to find a best price.

what_goes_wrong: `float('nan') != float('nan')` is true (a NaN never equals even itself). Worse, Python's `max([nan, 1])` returns `nan`, but `max([1, nan])` - the same two values in the other order - returns `1`: whichever element happens to be compared against the running maximum first determines whether the NaN "wins". JavaScript's `Math.max` doesn't have this order sensitivity - it returns `NaN` regardless of where the NaN sits in the argument list.
why: By IEEE 754, every comparison involving NaN (`<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `==`) returns false. Python's built-in `max`/`min` are implemented as a linear scan that keeps a running best value and replaces it only when `candidate > running_best` is true; since any comparison against a NaN is false, the running best only changes to NaN if NaN happens to be the very first element compared (so it never gets replaced), but if NaN appears later, `nan > current_best` is false, so the NaN is skipped and the earlier value is kept. JavaScript's `Math.max` is specified to return NaN if any argument is NaN, checked independently of ordering, which is why it doesn't show the same asymmetry.

repros.code:
nan = float("nan")
print(nan != nan)
print(max([nan, 1]), max([1, nan]))
print(min([nan, 1]), min([1, nan]))

fix: Filter out NaN values before calling max()/min() (e.g. `math.isnan`/`Number.isNaN`), rather than relying on max/min to handle them - and never use `==`/`!=` to check for a missing or invalid price; test for NaN explicitly.

sources.title: IEEE 754-2019 (comparison predicates involving NaN, summarized in Python's math module docs)

test_cases.note: A their_best_price(prices) function over price strings that may include an unparseable/NaN entry must give the same answer whatever order the list is in (filter or reject NaN explicitly); Python's max() over the floats gives nan for one order and 1.0 for the other.
